title: America Lost Its Measles Elimination Status. It’s a Tragedy.
summary: America has officially lost its measles elimination status.

“I started my training 20 years ago in India,” Dr. Sunil Muthusami, a pediatric hospitalist at a community hospital in Lancaster, Pa., told me. “I saw measles there. I did not think I was going to come here and see measles.” His hospital, which is near the epicenter of the largest active measles outbreak in the United States, has seen more than a dozen children come in with pneumonia, respiratory failure and brain inflammation as a result of the disease.


The hospital’s newborn intensive care unit had to open what’s known as a negative pressure unit — a space with specialized ventilation that is part of the most intense form of hospital infection control — to prevent the spread of measles. The children whose brains are affected (suggesting the virus may be causing neurological infection or inflammation) or who need ventilators are transferred to other hospitals that have pediatric intensive care units.


In 2000, the United States achieved measles elimination status. This milestone, defined by having no persistent transmission of the virus for more than 12 months, was the result of decades of work, including vaccine mandates in schools. Now, with more than 5,400 confirmed cases of measles reported so far this year, hundreds hospitalized and 10 deaths, we have joined a handful of countries that have officially[lost that status](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/17/well/us-measles-elimination-status.html) as a result of persistent transmission. This is a moral and medical tragedy, as well as a political failure.


You can talk about smallpox, as I do in my undergraduate classes, with a comfortable sense of curiosity and progress: That was terrible, and now it’s gone *.* The moral of the story is that international cooperation and scientific progress eliminated a terrible source of human suffering. When I was training in pediatrics in Boston in the 1980s, we couldn’t quite feel that way about measles, but we felt as though we were on our way, thanks to public health and a country that wanted its children to be safe. This essay is an elegy for a lost epidemiologic status, but also for that feeling — and for the people who are dying so unnecessarily now.


Measles ­could theoretically be eliminated from the planet, like smallpox was. As with smallpox, measles infects only humans, and we have a safe and effective vaccine. But measles is much more infectious than smallpox, so if it still exists in the world and we give it a foothold by having a population that is not fully vaccinated, it will come back, hanging in the air on the bus even after an infected person gets off, pervading an elementary school classroom or a sports stadium.


Dr. Muthusami told me that when families come in with a very sick child, often from Amish communities, they frequently report that the entire family has had the virus. Though the Amish faith does not forbid vaccination, its adherents have vaccination rates below the U.S. average, in part because many Amish people do not engage with the traditional medical system or do not trust it. Dr. Muthusami suspects that reports on the number infected undercount the amount of virus “actually out there.” He worries about children who seem to recover but can get sick again later. That’s because measles can suppress the immune system for months or years, and leaves patients at higher risk for severe infections, like pneumonia and sepsis.
